conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same. Helpers: isFirstBarOfSession(n) = bar[n] is the first bar of its trading day/session; bullTrendBar(n)/bearTrendBar(n) = body-fraction test; doji(n) = body(n) fraction of range below a small threshold; openingRangeHigh/openingRangeLow(openingRangeBars) = highest/lowest over the first N bars of the session; averageDailyRange(N) = average of (high-low) over the N prior sessions; priorSessionClose/High/Low = yesterday's session close/high/low; yesterdayClosingRangeHigh/Low(closingRangeBars) = highest/lowest of the last M bars of yesterday's session; consecutiveTrendBarSpike(startOffset, n, dir) = n consecutive trend bars in direction dir starting at bar[startOffset], each passing the trend-bar body test with limited bar-to-bar overlap.

candidates.name: IsFirstBarOfSession
candidates.quote: Institutional traders have orders to fill before the day opens, and they want to fill them at the best possible price.
candidates.description: Shared primitive (redefined here per chapter convention, see also V17-01): the current bar is the first bar of the session, i.e. its session date differs from the prior bar's.
notes: Structural helper needed by several candidates in this chapter.

candidates.name: ConsecutiveTrendBarSpike
candidates.quote: if there is a gap up or down and then a three- or four-bar bear spike within the first hour and the trend bars are large with little overlap and only small tails, the odds of a bear trend day increase.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: N consecutive trend bars in the same direction, each with body at least bodyFraction of its range and minimal overlap with the bar before it -- a 'spike'.
candidates.pseudocode: consecutiveTrendBarSpike(0, spikeBars, up) := for k in 0..spikeBars-1: (close[k] > open[k] && (close[k]-open[k]) >= bodyFraction*(high[k]-low[k]) && (k == spikeBars-1 || low[k] >= low[k+1] - maxOverlapTicks*tick))

complexity.reason: a fixed-length loop over consecutive bars applying a per-bar trend-bar test plus a bar-to-bar overlap test; no pivot detection needed

notes: Brooks uses this with spikeBars=2 for a lighter 'always-in' read and spikeBars=3-4 for a stronger trend-day read; both are captured by parameterizing spikeBars rather than by two separate primitives.

candidates.name: AlwaysInFromTwoConsecutiveTrendBars
candidates.quote: Traders often look for a pair of consecutive bull trend bars in the first hour or so. If they are present, traders would see them as a sign that the market is always-in long, at least for a scalp.
candidates.description: Two consecutive bull trend bars in the first hour set an always-in-long bias (context filter enabling with-trend long scalps/pullback entries).

complexity.reason: instance of V19-02 with spikeBars fixed at 2

candidates.name: GapPlusSpikeImpliesTrendDayBias
candidates.quote: if there is a gap up or down and then a three- or four-bar bear spike within the first hour and the trend bars are large with little overlap and only small tails, the odds of a bear trend day increase.
candidates.description: A session that opens with a gap and is immediately followed by a 3-4 bar trend-bar spike in the gap's direction raises the odds of a trend day in that direction -- a context filter favoring with-trend entries for the rest of the session.
candidates.pseudocode: (ctx.SessionDate(spikeBars) != ctx.SessionDate(spikeBars+1)) && low[spikeBars] > high[spikeBars+1] && consecutiveTrendBarSpike(0, spikeBars, up)

complexity.reason: combines the session-boundary primitive, a gap test, and the multi-bar spike primitive; 'increases the odds' is itself a soft bias rather than a hard threshold

notes: Brooks gives no numeric probability here beyond 'the odds increase'.

candidates.name: PullbackEntryAfterConsecutiveTrendBars
candidates.quote: if there have been consecutive strong bear trend bars and then a bar trades above the high of the prior bar, many traders will short below the low of that pullback bar for a scalp.
candidates.description: After a consecutive-bear-trend-bar spike, the first bar that trades above the high of the prior bar is a pullback bar: enter short one tick below that pullback bar's low (mechanized as close-then-next-open).
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick below the pullback bar's low (short) / above its high (long)

complexity.reason: the spike primitive plus a single fixed-offset comparison for the pullback bar

notes: This is a trend-continuation ('H2/L2'-style) entry; likely overlaps with a named counting-setup primitive from the trilogy's counting chapters not in this book.

candidates.name: WaitForDoubleTopBottomBeforeSwingEntry
candidates.quote: The high of the day usually comes from some kind of double top... and the low of the day usually comes from a double bottom... In general, if the day is having reversals, a trader should wait until there is a double top or bottom before looking for a swing trade.
candidates.description: Context filter: in a day showing multiple reversals, only size a trade for a swing target once a double top or double bottom has formed; before that, treat reversal entries as scalps only.

complexity.reason: depends on a double-top/double-bottom detection primitive (swing-pivot based), expected to be defined in this book's earlier reversal chapters (e.g. double top/bottom pullbacks)

notes: isDoubleTop/isDoubleBottom are placeholders for the primitive defined elsewhere in this book (chapter 8, not in this mining batch).

candidates.name: DojiFirstBarInYesterdayClosingRangeRangeDayBias
candidates.quote: If the first bar is a doji bar in the middle of yesterday's closing range, then the bar is a one-bar trading range, and the odds of a trading range day are increased.
candidates.description: Context filter: the first bar of the session is a doji and its range sits inside (near the middle of) yesterday's closing range -- raises the odds of a range day, favoring fade/mean-reversion setups over breakout entries.
candidates.pseudocode: (ctx.SessionDate(0) != ctx.SessionDate(1)) && (high[0]-low[0]) <= dojiRangeFraction*avgRange(rangeLookback) && abs(close[0]-open[0]) <= dojiBodyFraction*(high[0]-low[0]) && low[0] >= yesterdayClosingRangeLow(closingRangeBars) && high[0] <= yesterdayClosingRangeHigh(closingRangeBars)

complexity.reason: combines the session-boundary primitive, a doji test, and a comparison against a fixed prior window's high/low

notes: 'Middle of yesterday's closing range' is read as fully contained within it; Brooks gives no exact bar count for the closing range, so closingRangeBars=5 is a guess.

candidates.name: SmallOpeningRangeBreakoutBias
candidates.quote: If the range is only about 25 percent of the size of the range of recent days, traders will enter on a breakout of the range in either direction.
candidates.description: When the opening range (first N bars of the session) is small relative to the recent average daily range, bias toward taking breakout entries of that range in either direction (elevated trend-from-open odds).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter; the actual breakout order is OpeningRangeBreakoutTrendDay-style)

complexity.reason: a fixed opening-range window compared against a rolling average range; no pivot detection

notes: Pairs with the opening-range-breakout entry mined in chapter 18 (V18-02); this candidate supplies the 'is the range small enough to expect a clean breakout' precondition.

candidates.name: LargeOpeningRangeSpikeOrClimaxBias
candidates.quote: The third possibility is when the opening move is large. This is usually due to a strong spike and the day often becomes a spike and channel trend day, but sometimes it leads to a climactic reversal, usually after a small final flag.
candidates.description: When the opening range/move is large relative to the recent average daily range, bias toward expecting a spike-and-channel trend day (or, less often, a climactic reversal after a small final flag) rather than a contained trading range.

complexity.reason: same measurement as V19-08 with the opposite threshold direction

notes: The 'about a third to a half' medium regime in between V19-08 and this candidate is not encoded separately: its actionable content (breakout to a measured move, test of the breakout point, possible reversal day) duplicates already-mined breakout/measured-move concepts, so it is left as the implicit complement of V19-08/V19-09.

candidates.name: StrongInitialMoveMayReturnLaterFilter
candidates.quote: if the market sells off strongly for the first four bars of the day and then reverses up into a strong bull trend, you should remember the initial bear trend and not assume that the bulls will control the market until the close.
candidates.description: Context filter: after a strong opening move reverses into an opposite trend, do not fully discount the original direction -- keep a reduced-confidence bias that it could reassert later in the session (e.g. relaxing the always-in-long filter's exclusivity, or being quicker to accept a later bear signal).
candidates.pseudocode: consecutiveTrendBarSpike(sessionAge, spikeBars, down) /* the original spike, now sessionAge bars in the past */
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (soft bias filter, not an order)

complexity.reason: 'may return later in the day' has no concrete trigger condition in the text; a design decision is needed for what re-arms this bias and when it expires

notes: Recorded at high recall per instructions even though it is closer to a trading heuristic than a decidable test.

candidates.name: ReversalAtDefinedSupportResistanceLevel
candidates.quote: Look for reversals at support or resistance areas like the moving average, trend lines, trend channel lines, swing highs and lows (especially the high and low of yesterday), breakout areas, trading range tops and bottoms, and measured move targets.
candidates.description: Meta-filter: opening reversal setups cluster where price meets one of several defined support/resistance references (EMA, trend line, trend channel line, swing high/low -- especially yesterday's --, a breakout level, a trading-range boundary, or a measured-move target); a reversal-bar signal there is more credible than one in open space.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(close[0] - ema[0]) <= levelTouchTicks*tick || abs(close[0] - priorSessionHigh) <= levelTouchTicks*tick || abs(close[0] - priorSessionLow) <= levelTouchTicks*tick /* additional level terms: trend line, channel line, trading-range boundary, measured-move target -- each defined elsewhere */
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter enabling other reversal-entry candidates)

complexity.reason: several of the named levels (trend line, trend channel line, trading-range boundary, measured-move target) need pivot detection and line/measured-move projection; only the EMA and yesterday's-high/low terms are simple

notes: Deliberately composite/high-level: the authoring pass should decompose this into the individual level-touch primitives it lists, most of which belong to other chapters.

candidates.name: BreakoutModeStraddleEntry
candidates.quote: As soon as the market traded below bar 3, it became a spike up (a reversal down). Once the market traded above bar 4, it became a spike down (a reversal up). At that point, many traders treated those two spikes as a breakout mode setup and placed buy stops at one tick above the top spike and sell stops at one tick below the bottom spike.
candidates.description: After two opposing failed micro-spikes establish a small range within the opening range, place a resting stop order one tick above the range top (long) and one tick below the range bottom (short); whichever fills is the entry, and the other level becomes the initial protective stop.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] == highest(high, breakoutModeBars) && low[breakoutModeBars] == lowest(low, breakoutModeBars) /* placeholder: range top and bottom set by the two opposing failed spikes */ && close[0] > rangeTop
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the range top / sell stop one tick below the range bottom; the unfilled side becomes the protective stop

complexity.reason: requires detecting two opposing failed micro-spikes to fix the range boundaries, not a fixed lookback window

notes: This is the generic 'breakout mode' pattern, likely already defined as a primitive elsewhere in the trilogy (e.g. the trading-ranges volume); recorded here as it is stated in this chapter's opening-range context.

candidates.name: WidenStopAndPlanReversalOnAdverseMove
candidates.quote: If after entering, the market reverses direction, a trader will often double the size of the protective stop and plan to reverse the position if the stop is hit.
candidates.description: If price moves against a fresh position (toward the initial protective stop) without hitting it, widen the stop to a larger multiple of the original risk and, if that wider stop is subsequently hit, exit and reverse the position.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() != 0 && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < 0 && ctx.EntryPrice() - low[0] >= adverseMoveTicks*tick /* widen stop to stopWidenMultiple * initialRisk, and reverse if hit */
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (stop-adjustment and reversal management, not the original order type)

complexity.reason: reads position state (entry price, open profit) and adjusts a stop distance, then conditionally reverses -- cross-bar state but no pivot detection

notes: The reversal-on-widened-stop-hit half of this is really a Switch/re-entry permission; kept together here since the book states it as one management decision.

candidates.name: RepeatedFailedFollowThroughWeakness
candidates.quote: there were three bear trend bars before bar 4 and each was followed by a bar with a bull body. The bears were unable to create follow-through selling, which meant that they were weak.
candidates.description: Context filter: over the last N attempts, each bear trend bar was immediately followed by a bull-bodied bar (no follow-through selling) -- a sign of bear weakness that favors the opposite (bull) side.
candidates.pseudocode: countIf(k=1..lookback, close[k] < open[k] && close[k-1] > open[k-1]) >= weaknessCount
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: counting a two-bar failure pattern across a variable-length recent window is a pattern-recognition test, not a fixed-offset comparison

notes: The specific counts (three attempts, six-bar lookback) are readings of the single narrated example, not numbers Brooks generalizes.

candidates.name: TimeOfDayReversalWindow
candidates.quote: the trader needs to be aware that the market often reverses around 8:30 a.m. PST, and be prepared to take the trade.
candidates.description: Context filter: bars whose close time falls within a window around a known scheduled-report time (e.g. 8:30 a.m. exchange-adjusted) carry elevated odds of a trend start or reversal, regardless of whether it is still 'the opening range'.

complexity.reason: a plain bar-close-time comparison, though the specific time is exchange/market-dependent (U.S. economic data releases at 8:30 a.m. ET/PST-quoted here)

notes: The underlying reason (scheduled economic reports) is data the engine does not have, but the clock-time pattern itself is directly decidable from the bar timestamp, close to the existing TimeWindow rule shape.

rejected.quote: Institutional traders have orders to fill before the day opens... This creates a sell vacuum, and the market can move down quickly since the institutional bulls are simply waiting to buy at a more favorable price.
rejected.reason: requires knowledge of unobservable institutional order-flow intentions, not decidable from OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: When retail investors controlled a bigger part of the daily volume, they contributed more to opening gaps and reversals by placing orders before the open, based on the daily chart.
rejected.reason: historical market-structure commentary about past participant composition, not a present bar-level test

rejected.quote: The first bar of the day has about a 20 percent chance of being either the high or the low of the day for all markets... beginners struggle to determine which of the often several setups is that best one.
rejected.reason: descriptive statistics about outcome frequency, not an if-X-then-enter/exit statement

rejected.quote: Bar 3 was a double top with bar 1 and therefore had about a 50 percent chance of being the high of the day... Bar 7 broke a micro trend line and then bar 9 was a lower low breakout pullback buy setup.
rejected.reason: extended bar-by-bar figure narration (Figures 19.1-19.9) is discretionary chart commentary on specific historical charts; the recurring named patterns it applies (low 1/low 2, high 2, double top/bottom flags, barbwire, micro trend lines, ii patterns, wedges, climactic reversal, triangle) are primitives expected from other chapters of this book, not redefined here

chapter_summary: Explains why opening reversals happen (institutional order imbalances -- rejected as unobservable) and gives several mechanizable context filters for the opening range: consecutive-trend-bar spikes as an always-in signal (at different bar counts for a light vs. strong read), a doji-in-yesterday's-range first bar and small opening ranges as range-day/breakout-day classifiers, size-of-opening-range-vs-average-range as a three-way regime filter, waiting for a double top/bottom before sizing a swing, a generic 'reversal happens at a defined support/resistance level' meta-filter, a breakout-mode straddle-entry pattern, a stop-widen-and-reverse risk rule, and a scheduled-report time-of-day filter. Most of the back half of the chapter (pages 406-421) is bar-by-bar narration across nine figures reusing named patterns (low 1/low 2, high 2, double top/bottom flags, barbwire, ii patterns, micro trend lines, wedges, climactic reversal, triangles) that belong to other chapters of this book and were not redefined here; the dedup pass should expect this chapter's contribution to be the fifteen candidates above, several of them soft/research-grade context filters rather than hard entry triggers.
